title: The Science Behind Haldi Doodh: Why Turmeric Milk May Improve Your Sleep
excerpt: The ancient Indian drink combines anti-inflammatory curcumin with calming spices, and modern research is beginning to validate what generations of Indian families already knew.
body:
• Haldi doodh — turmeric milk — is an ancient Ayurvedic drink that Indian families have used for centuries as a home remedy and bedtime ritual
  • Curcumin, turmeric's active compound, has documented anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and immune-boosting properties backed by clinical research
  • Black pepper significantly improves curcumin absorption and is essential to getting the drink's full health benefits
  • While not a proven cure for insomnia, drinking golden milk before bed works as a calming ritual that many find helps with relaxation and sleep quality

Long before golden milk became a café menu staple in Brooklyn and London, Indian households had a simpler name for it: haldi doodh. A warm cup of turmeric-spiced milk at bedtime is a tradition spanning generations across the subcontinent, used as a home remedy for everything from sore throats to restless nights. A growing body of research is now catching up to what Indian families have practised for centuries.

What Goes in the Cup

At its simplest, haldi doodh is warm milk with turmeric. Traditional recipes add black pepper, ginger, cinnamon and sometimes cardamom or saffron. The drink varies from household to household and region to region across India, but the core — turmeric in warm milk — stays constant.

According to Sutter Health, golden milk is "deeply rooted in Ayurvedic medicine" and has been traditionally indicated as a cold-weather drink for cough and cold season. The basic recipe calls for half a teaspoon of turmeric powder, a pinch of black pepper, ginger and cinnamon in a cup of simmering milk. If adding honey, Ayurvedic tradition recommends waiting for the milk to cool first, as honey is not meant to be heated or boiled.

What Research Shows

The health interest in golden milk centres on curcumin, the compound that gives turmeric its distinctive yellow colour. A review published in the journal Foods found that curcumin has significant anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, with potential benefits for conditions ranging from arthritis to metabolic syndrome and anxiety.

An 18-month clinical trial among 40 adults found that participants taking curcumin supplements showed significantly improved memory and attention compared to a placebo group, with brain scans supporting the cognitive findings. Separately, a meta-analysis of 10 studies found curcumin effective at reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety.

On the immunity front, research has demonstrated curcumin's antibacterial, antiviral and antifungal properties — lending scientific support to the traditional use of haldi doodh during cold and flu season. A study comparing turmeric to omeprazole, a common heartburn medication, found turmeric offered comparable relief for indigestion at both 28 and 56 days of treatment.

"Golden Milk is a wonderful traditional aid for sleep that I often make myself. The ritual of making it is wonderful."

— Cara Marrs, Registered Dietitian Nutritionist, UCHealth

The Sleep Connection

The bedtime ritual is where golden milk has its most devoted following. While there is no conclusive scientific evidence that turmeric directly induces sleep, the drink works through several complementary mechanisms. Warm dairy milk contains tryptophan, an amino acid that supports relaxation. The ritual of preparing and sipping a warm drink signals wind-down time to the body. And curcumin's anti-inflammatory properties may help reduce the low-grade inflammation that can disrupt sleep quality.

Ayurvedic practitioners sometimes recommend adding a pinch of nutmeg to the bedtime version, as nutmeg can cause mild drowsiness. Sutter Health specifically notes this addition for those seeking better sleep. Ultimately, experts say there is no single best time of day to drink golden milk — some prefer it in the morning as a caffeine-free alternative to coffee — but the calming bedtime version remains the most popular choice.

Getting the Most From Your Cup

One detail often lost in trendy café versions: black pepper is not optional. Curcumin is poorly absorbed by the body on its own, but piperine — the compound in black pepper — dramatically improves absorption. A golden milk without pepper delivers little of the compound's health benefits.

The fat in whole milk also aids curcumin absorption, which is why traditional recipes call for full-fat dairy rather than water-based preparations. Plant-based milks work as alternatives, though they may not deliver all the same properties as the cow's milk version.

Turmeric is generally safe and well-tolerated. Most research shows no adverse effects even at high doses, though some people may experience mild digestive discomfort with large amounts. Those with dairy sensitivities should note that the milk component can trigger nighttime heartburn — somewhat counterproductive for a sleep drink.

An Old Tradition, Newly Validated

For the Indian diaspora, haldi doodh needs no rebranding. It is the drink your mother made when you had a cold, the one your grandmother swore would fix everything. What has changed is that Western medicine is starting to agree, at least on some of the claims. Whether you call it golden milk or haldi doodh, a warm cup before bed remains one of the simplest and most affordable wellness rituals available.
